h1: Foreign extra stout and tropical stout for hot climates
title: Foreign Extra and Tropical Stout | Craft Beer School
desc: What foreign extra stout and tropical stout are, how they were built for hot climates and how they differ from dry and imperial stout.
teaser: Stouts brewed stronger to survive long voyages and hot countries. India's climate is exactly what they were made for.
standfirst: When people think of stout, they picture a light, dry pint in a cool Irish pub. Two other stout styles grew up in warmer places: foreign extra stout and tropical stout. Here is how they differ and why they suit hot weather.
sections:
In the 18th and 19th centuries, British and Irish brewers shipped beer across the world to colonies and trading posts in Africa, Asia and the Caribbean. Weak beer did not survive long sea voyages in heat. Brewers made export versions stronger and more heavily hopped, so alcohol and hops would help protect the beer.

Those export stouts became foreign extra stout. Over time, local breweries in tropical countries made their own, often sweeter, versions. These became known as tropical stout. Both styles are recognised in the BJCP guidelines.

Foreign extra stout is very dark, usually black, with roughly 6.3 to 8% ABV. It is stronger and fuller than dry stout, with more roast, more bitterness or both. Flavours include roasted grain, coffee, dark chocolate and sometimes a slightly acidic tang. Some versions lean bitter and dry. Others are richer and sweeter.

The style varies by market. Some versions are brewed with local adjuncts. Breweries in parts of West Africa, for instance, use local sorghum in some stouts.

Tropical stout is sweeter and fruitier. It comes from the Caribbean, Sri Lanka and other warm regions, typically 5.5 to 8% ABV. It has a smooth, rich body, roasted coffee and chocolate flavours and a noticeable sweetness, often with dark fruit esters.

Bitterness is lower than in foreign extra stout. The sweetness balances the roast and makes the beer feel round and full.
How they compare with other stouts

• Dry stout is lighter, around 4 to 5% ABV, very dry and roasty.
  • Sweet or milk stout uses lactose for sweetness and is usually lower in alcohol. Our milk and oatmeal stout guide covers it.
  • Imperial stout is much stronger, about 8 to 12% ABV, with intense roast and dark fruit. Our imperial stout guide covers it.

Foreign extra and tropical stouts sit in the middle: stronger and richer than dry stout but lighter than imperial.

Both styles start from a stout grist of pale malt with roasted barley, chocolate or black malt, but in larger amounts than a dry stout so the original gravity lands higher. Foreign extra stout often carries a firmer hop charge, which brings the bitterness closer to the roast. Some brewers add a small amount of sugar to raise strength without making the body heavy.

Tropical stout leans on more caramel malt, sugar or adjuncts and a yeast that leaves more sweetness and fruit behind. Fermentation in warm climates historically ran warmer, which pushed up fruity esters. Modern brewers control that more tightly, but a little dark fruit remains part of the style.

Colour in both comes from roasted grain, so the balance between roast and smoothness depends on how much of it is used and how dark it is. Too much black malt and the beer tastes ashy. Too little and it tastes thin and sweet.

Higher alcohol, more hops and a robust malt base all help these beers stay stable when storage is warm. That matters in India, where beer often travels long distances without a reliable cold chain. A light, delicate beer shows staling quickly in heat. A stronger, darker beer hides it better.

They are also satisfying in warm weather when served properly. A tropical stout at 6 to 8 °C feels rich but refreshing. A foreign extra stout at 8 to 10 °C shows more roast and complexity.
Buying and storing them in India

Imported versions travel a long way and may sit in warm godowns. Their strength protects them better than a light lager, but a bottle kept at 35 °C for months will still lose roast character and turn flat or sherry like. Buy from shops that store beer cool and check the packaging date where one is printed.

At home, keep them in the fridge or the coolest dark cupboard you have. Store bottles upright. A few Indian craft breweries brew stronger stouts in winter. A fresh local stout is often a better example of what these styles taste like than a tired import.

The roast and sweetness suit grilled and smoky food. Try them with tandoori chicken, seekh kebabs, mutton chops, pork ribs or barbecue. Tropical stout's sweetness goes well with Goan pork dishes, jerk style chicken or a spicy Sri Lankan curry. Both pair well with dark chocolate, coffee desserts and plum cake.

If you can find both styles, taste them side by side with a dry stout. Notice the steps up in sweetness, body and alcohol. Then notice how roast feels different in each. Telling roast bitterness from hop bitterness is a key tasting skill. Those differences take practice to describe with confidence.
faqs: What is the difference between foreign extra stout and tropical stout?
Foreign extra stout is often more bitter and roasty. Tropical stout is sweeter and fruitier, with lower bitterness.
Higher alcohol and more hops helped the beer survive long sea voyages and hot climates.
Is tropical stout the same as milk stout?
No. Tropical stout gets its sweetness from malt and fermentation rather than lactose. It is usually stronger too.
